title: Efficiency — getting more out of what you put in
examTip: Efficiency has no units. It is a ratio between 0 and 1 (or 0–100%). Always check whether the question wants a decimal or a percentage.
introTips: No machine is ever 100% efficient. Some energy always leaks away as heat or sound.
A higher efficiency number means less energy is wasted.
You can work out efficiency using energy (joules) or power (watts). It is the same formula and the same answer.
intro: Imagine you pay for 100 units of electricity and only get 25 units of useful motion. That is a petrol car engine. Or you pay for 100 units and get 90 units of light. That is an LED. Efficiency tells you how good a device is at turning input energy into something useful. It matters because wasted energy costs money. It also uses up resources faster and adds to climate change. Efficiency is why LEDs replaced filament bulbs. It is why electric vehicles are gaining ground over petrol cars. It is also why energy ratings on appliances really matter.

keyPoints.heading: What efficiency means
keyPoints.content: Efficiency is the proportion of input energy that is usefully transferred. No real machine is 100% efficient. Some energy is always wasted, usually as thermal energy (heat) or sound. The equation is: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy. You can also give it as a percentage: efficiency = (useful output ÷ total input) × 100%. Efficiency has no units. It is a pure ratio (or percentage). The highest possible efficiency is 1.0 (or 100%). That would be a machine that wastes nothing. A machine with efficiency 0.75 transfers 75% of its input energy usefully. It wastes 25% to heat, sound or other stores we don't want.
writeBullets: Efficiency — the fraction of input energy that is usefully transferred. No units, between 0 and 1
Useful output energy — energy transferred to the store we want
Total input energy — all the energy supplied to the device, including what is wasted
Efficiency as a decimal — useful output ÷ total input (for example, 0.75)
Efficiency as a percentage — (useful output ÷ total input) × 100% (for example, 75%)

keyTerms.def: The proportion of input energy that is usefully transferred; efficiency = useful output ÷ total input
Energy transferred to the intended output store — the energy that does the job we want
All energy supplied to a device, including both useful and wasted portions

keyPoints.memTip: Efficiency = useful ÷ total. Think 'useful over all'.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to mix up useful output and total input. The total input is always the bigger number.

keyPoints.heading: Calculating efficiency
keyPoints.content: The efficiency equation works with both energy (in joules) and power (in watts): - efficiency = useful output energy (J) ÷ total input energy (J) - efficiency = useful output power (W) ÷ total input power (W) Worked example 1: a motor gets 500 J of electrical energy. It does 375 J of useful mechanical work → efficiency = 375 ÷ 500 = 0.75 (75%). Worked example 2: an LED bulb uses 10 W of electrical power. It gives out 9 W of useful light → efficiency = 9 ÷ 10 = 0.9 (90%). Worked example 3: a petrol car engine has an input power of 100 kW. It gives out 25 kW of kinetic energy → efficiency = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 (25%). The other 75 kW is wasted as thermal energy and sound. You can also rearrange it: - useful output = efficiency × total input - total input = useful output ÷ efficiency
writeBullets: Efficiency = useful output energy (J) ÷ total input energy (J). Works with joules
Efficiency = useful output power (W) ÷ total input power (W). Works with watts too
Rearrangement: useful output = efficiency × total input
Rearrangement: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency
Converting to %: multiply the decimal efficiency by 100

keyTerms.def: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy (or useful power ÷ total input power)
Total input energy minus useful output energy — always positive in a real device

keyPoints.memTip: Worked examples: motor 375/500=0.75; LED 9/10=0.9; car engine 25/100=0.25. Practise these numbers.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Always write out the formula first. Then substitute, then calculate. This picks up method marks even if the final answer is wrong.

keyPoints.heading: Comparing efficiencies of different devices
keyPoints.content: Real devices have very different efficiencies. Some are surprisingly poor. - LED bulbs: ~90% efficient (electrical → light). Excellent. - Fluorescent tubes: ~70–80% efficient. - Incandescent (filament) bulbs: only ~5% efficient. Most electrical energy goes to heat, and hardly any to light! - Electric motors: up to 90% efficient. - Petrol car engines: typically 25–30% efficient. Most energy is wasted as heat in the engine and exhaust. - Electric vehicles: ~85–90% efficient. The motor is very efficient, and regenerative braking recovers more energy. - Solar panels (photovoltaic): typically 15–20% efficient in everyday use. - The human body: about 25% efficient at turning chemical energy (food) into mechanical energy. The rest is thermal energy. That is why you get warm when you exercise.
writeBullets: LED bulb — ~90% efficient. Electrical energy → light, with very little wasted as heat
Incandescent bulb — only ~5% efficient. ~95% of the energy is wasted as thermal energy
Electric motor — up to ~90% efficient. Very good at turning electrical energy → kinetic energy
Petrol engine — ~25–30% efficient. Most energy is lost as thermal energy and sound
Electric vehicle — ~85–90% efficient. Much better than petrol, and helped by regenerative braking
Human body — ~25% efficient. Chemical energy (food) → mechanical energy + lots of heat

keyTerms.def: Old-style filament light bulb — only ~5% efficient, wastes most energy as heat
Light Emitting Diode — ~90% efficient at converting electrical energy to light

keyPoints.memTip: Remember the big contrast: LED ≈ 90% efficient, old filament bulb ≈ 5% efficient. That is why the switch mattered!
keyPoints.tutor_note: Comparing devices is a common exam question. Know rough efficiency values for LEDs and filament bulbs. Know them for electric and petrol vehicles too.

keyPoints.heading: Improving efficiency and energy ratings
keyPoints.content: We can improve efficiency in several ways: - Reducing friction: oil between moving parts → less kinetic energy wasted as thermal energy. - Better insulation: less thermal energy lost from hot surfaces to the surroundings. Insulating a boiler is one example. - More efficient components: LEDs instead of filament bulbs, and electric motors instead of petrol engines. - Regenerative systems: these capture energy that would be wasted. Regenerative braking in EVs is an example. Energy efficiency labels: UK and EU appliances carry an A–G energy label. A is the most efficient, and G is the least. Very efficient appliances cost more to buy. But they use less electricity, which saves money on bills. Payback time = extra cost of the efficient appliance ÷ yearly saving on energy bills. Example: an efficient fridge costs £200 more than a cheap one. It saves £40/year → payback time = 200 ÷ 40 = 5 years.
writeBullets: Lubrication — reduces friction between moving parts, cutting wasted thermal energy
Insulation — slows thermal energy loss from hot surfaces to the surroundings
Efficient components — LEDs and electric motors use less energy for the same output
Regenerative braking — recovers kinetic energy instead of wasting it as heat
Energy label (A–G) — A is the most efficient. It helps buyers compare appliances
Payback time — extra cost ÷ annual saving. It tells you how long until the savings cover the higher price

keyTerms.def: A–G rating on UK/EU appliances showing how efficiently they use energy
Time for energy savings to cover the extra cost of a more efficient device; payback time = extra cost ÷ annual saving

keyPoints.memTip: Payback time = extra cost ÷ annual saving. Units: years.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Payback time questions often come up in 6-mark questions with efficiency. Know both formulas. Be able to judge whether an upgrade is worth it.

0.question: A device receives 800 J of energy and usefully transfers 560 J. What is its efficiency?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! efficiency = 560 ÷ 800 = 0.70 = 70%. The other 30% (240 J) is wasted.
0.wrongFeedback: Use efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = 560 ÷ 800 = 0.70. Multiply by 100 for a percentage: 70%.

1.question: An LED bulb and a filament bulb both use 60 W of electrical power. Which statement is correct?
options: The LED gives more useful light, because it is more efficient (~90% vs ~5%)
They give the same amount of light, because they use the same power
The filament bulb is more efficient, because it also gives out heat
The LED wastes more energy, because it runs cooler
1.correctFeedback: Exactly right! The LED turns ~90% of 60 W into light (~54 W of light). The filament bulb turns only ~5% into light (~3 W of light). Same input, very different useful output.
1.wrongFeedback: The same power input does NOT mean the same efficiency. The LED (~90% efficient) turns far more of its 60 W into useful light. The filament bulb (~5% efficient) wastes almost all its energy as heat.

3.question: A more efficient washing machine costs £150 more. It saves £30 per year on electricity bills. What is the payback time?
3.correctFeedback: Correct! Payback time = extra cost ÷ annual saving = £150 ÷ £30 = 5 years.
3.wrongFeedback: Payback time = extra cost ÷ annual saving = £150 ÷ £30 = 5 years. After 5 years, the savings have paid back the extra cost.

commonMistakes: Putting total input on top instead of useful output. Always put USEFUL output on top: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.
Thinking efficiency can be more than 1 (or 100%). That would break the conservation of energy. Always check your answer is ≤ 1.
Forgetting to convert between decimal and percentage. If a question asks for a percentage, multiply by 100.
Mixing up power efficiency and energy efficiency. They give the same result. Keep the units the same: both in W, or both in J.
Saying a device 'creates' or 'destroys' energy. It transfers energy. The total input always equals useful output + wasted energy.
examTips: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. Check: is the answer between 0 and 1? If not, you have divided the wrong way round.
You may be given power values instead of energy values. The same formula works: efficiency = useful output power ÷ total input power.
For payback time: payback time (years) = extra cost (£) ÷ annual saving (£/year). Always give the units.
When comparing devices, quote efficiency values. Explain what 'more efficient' means for energy transfer. Don't just say 'wastes less'.
